>From "Eli Zaretskii" <eliz@gnu.org>
To "ron li" <liyananfamily@gmail.com>
Cc emacs-devel@gnu.org
Date 06/11/2026 07:25:29
Subject Re: Native TTY image support in Emacs

>>  From: ron li <liyananfamily@gmail.com>
>>  Date: Thu, 5 Nov 2026 18:07:44 -0800
>>  Cc: emacs-devel@gnu.org
>>
>>  The image can still occupy several screen rows. Each row is one
>>  terminal cell high and shows a horizontal band of the same image.
>>  For example, after scrolling the first two rows out of view:
>>
>>      Before scrolling          After scrolling
>>      +----------------+        +----------------+
>>      | image band 1   |        | image band 3   |
>>      | image band 2   |        | image band 4   |
>>      | image band 3   |        | image band 5   |
>>      | image band 4   |        | image band 6   |
>>      | image band 5   |        | following text |
>>      | image band 6   |        |                |
>>      +----------------+        +----------------+
>>
>>  I verified partial visibility at both vertical window edges in Kitty.
>>
>>  I suggested insert-sliced-image because explicit slices let us test
>>  whether the existing fixed-height TTY rows can handle scrolling and
>>  clipping. If redisplay can lay out a regular image spec as these rows
>>  internally, insert-image would be the natural interface for callers.
>>  Does that sound like a reasonable direction?
>
>I think you misunderstand the main difficulty in adding this feature
>to Emacs.  The main difficulty is to modify and/or reconcile the
>current assumption that all screen lines (a.k.a. "glyph rows") on TTY
>frames have the same height whose "pixel height" is taken to be 1.
>This assumption is fundamental in all the TTY display code that deals
>with layout and anything that depends on the layout: vertical cursor
>movement, support for mouse, TTY menus, and much more.
>
>What you suggest doesn't by itself solve this fundamental problem,
>because image slices are just images: they still need to be laid out,
>each slice on its screen line.  In your diagram above, there's nothing
>to the left of the slices, which is impossible in Emacs without some
>magic (which is currently missing).  Suppose that a buffer's text is
>like this:
>
>   abcde <IMAGE> xyz
>
>Then, I presume you would want to display this as slices like this:
>
>         | image band 1   |
>         | image band 2   |
>         | image band 3   |
>         | image band 4   |
>         | image band 5   |
>   abcde | image band 6   | xyz
>
>Is that right?  In that case, the empty space to the left of all the
>slices except the last (bottom-most) one is a problem for the Emacs
>display engine, because there must be something there for us to be
>able to tell the terminal to show those slices.  We must write
>something, probably space characters, to the terminal from the left
>edge of the window till the beginning of the slice.  And we can only
>write those space characters if the corresponding glyph row has some
>glyphs there.  Those glyphs should probably be generated by the
>display code itself, because they don't correspond to any buffer text,
>but some code needs to be added to do it, and that code must be part
>of handling text with embedded images.
>
>In addition, with slices we will have hard time calculating the pixels
>in a way that will avoid gaps between slices on the screen.
>
>So I think we need either some additional tricks, like an ability to
>generate more than one screen line for a text line with embedded
>images, or do what Gerd suggested back in 2022: abandon the simplistic
>layout of TTY frames and teach Emacs to support variable-height glyph
>rows on TTYs.
>
>In both cases, I'm afraid it is not a trivial job, and will require
>studying the current display code and making non-trivial changes in
>it.  If you or anyone else are up to the job, I personally and others
>will be happy to provide advice and guidance.
>

>
> Assuming Augusto agrees, then vibe-spell is a fork+translation as
> opposed to just a transcompilation of an existing program.  The source
> code in vibe-spell.el is authoritative on its own and there is no
> expectation that C++ changes can be (automatically) copied over, as the
> translation is not a process that one would expect to repeat over and
> over (which is the case with C/C++->Bison or Org->Texinfo, considering
> that you know that the tool will overwrite your changes in the
> intermediate representations).

That's exactly how I see it.

Including the prompts in the package makes as much sense as including
any scrap of paper where someone sketched an algorithm; I don't even
have those prompts anymore.

Also, I'm not sure what is meant by "including the source" of Hunspell
and Nuspell, but those things are widely available.  One way to get them
is by the corresponding Makefile targets in the package.

As to legal implications, I have no idea if I'm required to credit the
Hunspell and Nuspell authors (the LLM had access to both codebases), or
whether I am bound by the copyleft clauses of those programs (I guess
nobody knows at this point).  This also makes no difference to me, as I
want to release the generated code under GPL and I don't particularly
care what string of text appears in the copyright attribution of the
package.

Clearly the package is not currently acceptable in GNU ELPA.

W.r.t NonGNU ELPA, as the discussion here shows, there's some unease
about whether we should accept such packages.

Originally, NonGNU was created for packages which we couldn't get to GNU
ELPA but which we thought were important to distribute.  This has
somewhat evolved over time and we're a bit more less demanding w.r.t the
"importance", but still in the case of Vibe-Spell, I think I lean
towards saying that there is not yet a clear sign of its importance
(while it provides a different tradeoff than Hunspell and Jinx,
those two alternatives are quite popular and have served us well enough
so far).  Hopefully, by the time it becomes more popular/important, we
will have more historical data about how maintenance of such code plays
out, which should help focus the discussion (tho I am not deluded
enough to think that discussion will not be heated).

> I don't mind, but I'll mention I've been using this for about a month
> myself, so I'd say the private stage of development has run its course.

FWIW, Github suggest the initial commit was on Oct 24, which is quite
a bit less than a month ago (tho it was admittedly "last month" 🙂).


=== Stefan


PS: I was careful above to try and avoid giving my opinion on the LLM
part of the matter, because I have not yet really formed a clear
opinion.  What I'll note is that what you describe as the process to
create Vibe-Spell smells to me like "copy&paste" (with some
transpilation thrown-in), so my immediate reaction is to worry about
propagating future bug-fixes and other changes from Hunspell to
Vibe-Spell.

I think we are leaving that period already.

I believe a generative LLM (I like to call that a "chatbot")
has no difficulties (in principle) to deliver one big hunk of
hot mess covering the "full stack" down to machine code.

It'll use up a couple o' more tokens, granted, but the "AI Lords"
will have to sell a lot of those if they want a chance to narrow
the yawning abism between investor cash burn and revenue.

> Even if the software itself does not get maintained long-term, its
> reliability depends on the libraries being reliable.
>=20
> That could explain why there=E2=80=99s so much pressure to make lax licen=
sed libraries.

Watch the npm space. I think we are currently leaving this model
behind us.

Not without some kicking and screaming, mind you :-)

Do the Emacs maintainers use LLMs?  If they don't, then it is technically
problematic, and inconsiderate towards the humans involved, whether
well-intentioned or not, to propose accepting LLM code when neither the
Emacs maintainers nor the GNU Project control what an LLM does, quite apart
from the legal and ethical issues of LLM-generated code.

And if forking is the way forward, why aren't those who want LLM-generated
code accepted in Emacs the ones proposing the fork?

> From: Augusto Stoffel <arstoffel@gmail.com>
> Cc: Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org>,  cwebber@dustycloud.org,  emacs-devel@gnu.org
> Date: Fri, 06 Nov 2026 10:09:20 +0100
> 
> 
> > Assuming Augusto agrees, then vibe-spell is a fork+translation as
> > opposed to just a transcompilation of an existing program.  The source
> > code in vibe-spell.el is authoritative on its own and there is no
> > expectation that C++ changes can be (automatically) copied over, as the
> > translation is not a process that one would expect to repeat over and
> > over (which is the case with C/C++->Bison or Org->Texinfo, considering
> > that you know that the tool will overwrite your changes in the
> > intermediate representations).
> 
> That's exactly how I see it.
> 
> Including the prompts in the package makes as much sense as including
> any scrap of paper where someone sketched an algorithm; I don't even
> have those prompts anymore.

So if you need to update the package with fixes and improvements
introduced in a future version of Hunspell, you will start the entire
conversion job from scratch?  If not, what will be the workflow for
such an update?

> Also, I'm not sure what is meant by "including the source" of Hunspell
> and Nuspell, but those things are widely available.  One way to get them
> is by the corresponding Makefile targets in the package.

The GPL requires that any distribution of a package includes all of
the sources which were used to produce the executable code.  That
means, among other things, the exact version of Hunspell which was the
starting point of the conversion must be available to people who
download and install your package.  You could make that version of
Hunspell available by pointing to some site which holds that exact
version, of course, but unless this site is Savannah or something
under our control, such pointers are unreliable because the source
tarball or repository to which you point might disappear some day.  So
"widely available" doesn't really satisfy these requirements; as the
very least you should tell which version of Hunspell was used and
where did you download it from.

> As to legal implications, I have no idea if I'm required to credit the
> Hunspell and Nuspell authors (the LLM had access to both codebases), or
> whether I am bound by the copyleft clauses of those programs (I guess
> nobody knows at this point).  This also makes no difference to me, as I
> want to release the generated code under GPL and I don't particularly
> care what string of text appears in the copyright attribution of the
> package.

Well, you should care.  But the main issue here is not attribution,
but what constitutes the source code of such a package.  Attribution
is a separate matter.  Since Hunspell is (AFAIK) GPL, you can
distributed derivative work based on it under GPL or compatible
license.  Again, that's not the issue I raised.

think that Emacs maintainers came up and suggested accepting
LLM-generated code.  That's not what happened.

On Thu, 5 Nov 2026 at 13:57, ron li <liyananfamily@gmail.com> wrote:


> I'd like to revisit the 2022 discussion on supporting existing Emacs
> image specs on text terminals, starting with Kitty graphics.
>

Out of curiosity, why are a lot of people so into using Emacs on a terminal
emulator?

I can understand you would want to use Emacs on a text terminal if that's
all you got. On the other hand, if your terminal emulator supports
displaying graphics, you are using a system that can display graphics, so
why cram the images through the virtual serial line?

Is the fact that modern terminal emulators run Emacs ten times faster than
as a GUI application the reason? If so, shouldn't we be working on
getting Emacs run faster with native graphics, instead of trying to escape
the straitjacket the terminal emulator is?

Is the reason that Emacs is often used on a remote machine via ssh?
Wouldn't it be better to use a windowing system version of Emacs and use
X11 forwarding or Waypipe to display it on the local screen?

X-List-Received-Date: Fri, 06 Nov 2026 13:35:05 -0000

> From: "Michael Grant" <mgrant@grant.org>
> Cc: emacs-devel@gnu.org
> Date: Fri, 06 Nov 2026 08:36:50 +0000
> 
> If I understand what Ron Li is aiming for here, he's referring to the 
> Kitty unicode placeholder images (described below).  Eli, in your 
> example below, the space to the left would be padded with space 
> characters in the buffer. But I think we are talking about different 
> things here.
> 
> There are 2 separate things: 1) displaying graphics in a terminal window 
> and 2) displaying files with embedded images or files which are an 
> image.  These are things at different levels.

These two cases are identical from Emacs's POV.  An image is
represented in an Emacs buffer as a special 'display' property, which
shows the image instead of the text which has that property.  Showing
a single image in a buffer is thus a special case of showing an image
embedded in text: in the former case you have only the text covered by
the 'display' property, in the latter case you also have text without
the property before and after the image.

The important aspect of this is that in both cases the Emacs display
engine needs to be able to lay out the text and the image in a way
that what's on the glass corresponds to what Emacs holds in its glyph
matrices.  This is needed so that Emacs could do stuff that requires
the layout information.  For example, C-n needs to compute the buffer
position on a screen line below the current one, and processing a
mouse click needs to determine the buffer position at the click point.

> I think Ron is talking about the display engine in emacs that would 
> convert the image to whatever the terminal supports.  There are at least 
> 3 supported ways to display images in the terminal (I would not be 
> surprised if there were more): Sixel which is old and widely supported 
> by VTxxx terminals, Kitty Image Protocol which is popular because of 
> Kitty Term, and Kitty Unicode Placeholders which is a second way Kitty 
> Terminal deals with images which is what I think Ron Li is thinking of.
> 
> As far as I can tell, Sixel and Kitty Image Protocol are similar in that 
> they blat out bits to display in the TTY.  The pixels stay on the TTY 
> screen, some TTYs scroll them around.
> 
> The Kitty Unicode Placeholder is different.  The image is "uploaded" to 
> the terminal once and each character shaped block of the image is 
> identified with a Unicode character: U+10EEEE, encoding the image ID in 
> the fg color. The row and column values are encoded in the diacritics.  
> Thus each cell (each character sized block of the image) has a unique 
> unicode "character" which, when emacs wants to tell the terminal this 
> character sized block of the image goes here, it sends that unicode 
> character to the terminal and the terminal outputs the intended block of 
> the image.

You are talking about how to deliver the image data to the terminal.
That needs to be implemented, of course, but it isn't the main
difficulty.  The main difficulty is to adapt the text-mode display
code to this situation, because images are rarely the same vertical
size as the characters shown on the terminal.

> But the thing I want to get across here is that all of these things are 
> how to display images in a terminal.  If you are mixing images and text, 
> that's a different problem.

Not in Emacs, it isn't.  It's the same problem.  Emacs still needs to
know the dimensions of the image on the glass, because otherwise Emacs
features that users expect to work with images will not work.

> If you have some file like some mime 
> document with embedded images, then I think you need some mode in emacs 
> that deals with those file types (maybe it exists already?) that when it 
> shows the image part of the file it outputs the image bits in sixels or 
> kitty graphics, or, it first uploads the image to the terminal using the 
> kitty placeholder and then outputs kitty unicode placeholders where it 
> wants to output those cells with images.

Again, you are talking about how to deliver the image data to the
terminal, whereas I'm talking about the layout calculations in the
presence of images.

Emacs maintains a data structure called "glyph matrix" for every
window on display.  That data structure is a 2D array of objects
called "glyphs"; each glyph describes a single "display element" on
the glass.  A display element can be a character, an image, a
composition (result of composing several characters, like a base
character and a diacritic), a stretch of white space, etc.  Each row
in the glyph matrix describes a single screen line.  To perform layout
calculations, Emacs needs to know the Y-coordinate of each glyph row
and the width of each glyph.  Currently, the text-mode display assumes
that each glyph has 1-pixel width and row number N (zero-based) has Y
coordinate equal to N.  Displaying images means these assumptions
cannot be true anymore.  The width issue can be handled relatively
easily (we already do something similar for wide characters that
occupy 2 columns on display).  The height issue is harder, because the
display code currently cannot generate several screen lines (= glyph
rows) from a single display element.

I hope the above explains what I think is the most complex part of the
job of adding image support to TTY frames.  If not, feel free to ask
questions.

saying that it only makes sense if human emacs will fork regardless of

the point, again, is that if gnu emacs accepts genai contributions, then
a fork is an inevitable consequence. as that is the sole issue at hand,
then what purpose would there be in an llm-free fork if gnu emacs is
pledged to be llm-free?

> No one explained what kind of hostility will happen, and people here,

indeed, i have decided that llms are, at every level, an affront to
justice, from who makes and profits and pushes them, to how they are
trained, to the resources used, to the way they are used, to what they
do to people who use them, to what they do to the communities where
their use is tolerated. everywhere, and in profound ways, i have looked
and seen llms as a destructive force that only exist to empower the few
at the incredible, immoral expense of the many.

in my view, while there may be some benefits to llms in some
circumstances, their harms vastly outweigh those, and, if i want to live
in accord with my principles of justice, i am left with no choice but to
reject them at every opportunity and in every way. i cannot come to
another conclusion based on my sense of ethics.

> That's very different.  Here, we are asked to reject a completely
> valid, free and correct code just because of its progeny.  It's like
> saying that code from left-handed or red-haired people should not be
> accepted.

my point is not the progeny, but that the gnu project often rejects
technically and legally valid contributions because of gnu
ideology. progeny can be factored into that.

as a hypothetical example: if i live in a territory that permits
slavery, and by law i am granted sole ownership of the products of that
forced labor, and then i use that to create contributions to gnu emacs,
complete with copyright assignment, and it is technically correct, and,
above all, you, the emacs maintainers are aware of how this was
produced, would it be ethical to accept those contributions?

it is my worry that the fsf and gnu's apparent narrow focus on legality
and technical correctness in the framing of llm contributions ignores
the much larger issues with supporting human freedom, and, as such,
becomes hypocritcal: free software is free in name only when it is used
for subjugation or created from subjugation.

this example is hypothetical and not intended to display any real or
imagined link to how llms are created and operated. it is only intended
as a philosophical point on how a narrow focus on license legality and
technical correctness are, at times, inadequate in the pursuit of the
larger goal of liberty for all humanity.

On Fri, 6 Nov 2026 at 17:43, Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> wrote:

> > Including the prompts in the package makes as much sense as including

> > have those prompts anymore.
>
> So if you need to update the package with fixes and improvements
> introduced in a future version of Hunspell, you will start the entire
> conversion job from scratch?  If not, what will be the workflow for
> such an update?

If you hand-translated Hunspell version X into Elisp and then version
Y were released and you wanted to update your Elisp translation, what
would the workflow be?

1. You read the diffs. Maybe not the whole diff X..Y; maybe you read
individual commits, or short patch series. You work out what they did
and how they did it.
2. Knowing your translation, you work out how to implement the changes
on top of it.
3. You run tests. Fix code until they pass.
4. You commit and push.

The LLM-assisted workflow is essentially the same. =E2=80=9CHey agent. ! gi=
t
-C ../hunspell log X..Y. Explain those changes to me.=E2=80=9D The agent th=
en
generates a bunch of tool calls to read the changes, read the context
around them, gives you the code tour. =E2=80=9CNow let=E2=80=99s port those=
 changes to
our ./vibespell.el.=E2=80=9D Reads the existing implementations, modifies t=
he
existing implementation, runs tests, until convergence. =E2=80=9CDone, test=
s
pass.=E2=80=9D You review the changes, =E2=80=9CHey, this chain of (nth =E2=
=80=A6) accesses
would look better as a pcase=E2=80=9D. =E2=80=94 =E2=80=9CYou=E2=80=99re ri=
ght, changed, tests pass.=E2=80=9D
You commit and push.

> Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:
> 
> > No one explained what kind of hostility will happen, and people here,
> > myself included, don't really understand what is alluded to.  It
> > almost seems like you've decided that LLMs have adverse effects in
> > some of their popular uses, and therefore using LLM-generated code
> > will somehow "infect" Emacs even though those problematic aspects of
> > using LLMs are completely irrelevant for our case.  I personally hope
> > that this is not the reason, but in the absence of any other
> > argumentation, what else is left?
> 
> indeed, i have decided that llms are, at every level, an affront to
> justice, from who makes and profits and pushes them, to how they are
> trained, to the resources used, to the way they are used, to what they
> do to people who use them, to what they do to the communities where
> their use is tolerated. everywhere, and in profound ways, i have looked
> and seen llms as a destructive force that only exist to empower the few
> at the incredible, immoral expense of the many.

So basically, you are saying that just because LLMs can and perhaps do
harm elsewhere, we should not let them anywhere near Emacs, regardless
of what they can or cannot do to Emacs and our community.

> in my view, while there may be some benefits to llms in some
> circumstances, their harms vastly outweigh those, and, if i want to live
> in accord with my principles of justice, i am left with no choice but to
> reject them at every opportunity and in every way. i cannot come to
> another conclusion based on my sense of ethics.

There's a lot of evil in this world, and we meet it all the time.  In
the Free Software movement, we only deal with evil that directly
affects or threatens software freedoms.  Fighting the rest should be
left for other arenas.

> > That's very different.  Here, we are asked to reject a completely
> > valid, free and correct code just because of its progeny.  It's like
> > saying that code from left-handed or red-haired people should not be
> > accepted.
> 
> my point is not the progeny, but that the gnu project often rejects
> technically and legally valid contributions because of gnu
> ideology. progeny can be factored into that.

No, progeny _cannot_ be factored into that.  It shouldn't be.  It must
not be.

> as a hypothetical example: if i live in a territory that permits
> slavery, and by law i am granted sole ownership of the products of that
> forced labor, and then i use that to create contributions to gnu emacs,
> complete with copyright assignment, and it is technically correct, and,
> above all, you, the emacs maintainers are aware of how this was
> produced, would it be ethical to accept those contributions?

Our answer must be YES.

Any other answer is a first step towards splitting our community along
the many lines of political and ideological divides that have nothing
to do with software freedoms.  Right now we have contributors from all
over the world, despite the differences in their regimes and political
systems, differences in ideologies, and even in the very
interpretation of the notion of "freedom".  You are suggesting to
subject the contributors to some examination of the principles they
uphold, the ethics of their day-to-day activities, their views on
matters of policies and important international events, etc.  This
will immediately fracture our community into many different enclaves.
And that's exactly my point, and the main reason why I must reject the
"Human Emacs" initiative, as it is presented to us.

> it is my worry that the fsf and gnu's apparent narrow focus on legality
> and technical correctness in the framing of llm contributions ignores
> the much larger issues with supporting human freedom, and, as such,
> becomes hypocritcal: free software is free in name only when it is used
> for subjugation or created from subjugation.

There's no hypocrisy here, only the realization and understanding that
we cannot fix everything in this world, even if we tried, not via
developing and distributing software.  So we limit ourselves to
solving a few of the problems, and leave the rest to other
communities.  (Of course, people who contribute to Emacs can well be
members of those other communities as well.)

> this example is hypothetical and not intended to display any real or
> imagined link to how llms are created and operated. it is only intended
> as a philosophical point on how a narrow focus on license legality and
> technical correctness are, at times, inadequate in the pursuit of the
> larger goal of liberty for all humanity.

The Free Software movement doesn't pursue the goal of "liberty for all
humanity".  If you think it does, you are gravely mistaken.  Our goals
are different, and are well described elsewhere.

>Emacs maintains a data structure called "glyph matrix" for every
>window on display.  That data structure is a 2D array of objects
>called "glyphs"; each glyph describes a single "display element" on
>the glass.  A display element can be a character, an image, a
>composition (result of composing several characters, like a base
>character and a diacritic), a stretch of white space, etc.  Each row
>in the glyph matrix describes a single screen line.  To perform layout
>calculations, Emacs needs to know the Y-coordinate of each glyph row
>and the width of each glyph.  Currently, the text-mode display assumes
>that each glyph has 1-pixel width and row number N (zero-based) has Y
>coordinate equal to N.  Displaying images means these assumptions
>cannot be true anymore.  The width issue can be handled relatively
>easily (we already do something similar for wide characters that
>occupy 2 columns on display).  The height issue is harder, because the
>display code currently cannot generate several screen lines (=3D glyph
>rows) from a single display element.

I am familiar with the glyph matrix from a character perspective.  By 1=20
pixel, i think you mean one character in the TUI which is usually=20
several pixels on the user's screen?  If there was an image in the glyph=20
matrix, is it a single cell in that matrix?  I realize this may not=20
apply to emacs but in tmux and with kitty's placeholder images, the=20
image spans multiple character cells.  tmux has something similar to the=20
glyph matrix, namely a grid of cells and if there is an image in the=20
tty, the x by y block of characters that the image covers are marked as=20
part of the image.  If Ron's idea is something like that where an image=20
is split into y lines of x wide character strips, then, it sounded a lot=20
like tmux's grid and it sounded like the glyph matrix might have worked=20
that way as well but it sounds like an image, no matter how large, sits=20
in a single glyph.

Anyway, I think I see Ron's idea of strips.  As long as those strips are=20
the same height as the characters which should be possible.  I guess=20
each strip becomes a glyph on a separate row?  There is an escape=20
sequence to know the geometry of characters on the TTY so this shouldn't=20
be difficult to know how to stripe the image.

If an image is a single glyph then if you represent the image as kitty=20
unicode placeholder characters, it does become like a wide character, or=20
in this case the single glyph image is represented by an x by y grid of=20
terminal characters, each of those characters are the unicode=20
placeholders.  Honestly, if that's the case then yeah, it's going to be=20
a bit painful to do this because if the vertical height issue you say.

By the way, regardless of whether you are running emacs in the terminal=20
or emacs in tmux in the terminal, it should be the same.  tmux supports=20
the kitty graphics protocol and sixels as many terminals do.  If you get=20
this to work on emacs -nw outside tmux, it should look the same as=20
running emacs -nw inside tmux.  If, when you implement this, you redraw=20
the image every time you scroll, you will see some flashing.  If emacs=20
is able to push the image around using the terminal's scrolling, then=20
it'll look much better, both in tmux and out.  I guess that statement=20
really applies to sixels and kitty images and not the kitty unicode=20
placeholder images.

Anyway, I don't think I'm being helpful here but I do think it should be=20
possible to display images in the TUI and all I ask is that it not be=20
inexctricably bound to kitty unicode placeholders, please keep the=20
display bit separate from the internal representation bit.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

  > An easier to convey example is with [Putative Intelligence]-art: if you tell [a PI] model
  > “make this blue”, it often doesn’t only make this blue, but adds other
  > changes. An art director explained a while back that this makes it
  > almost impossible for him to work with people who use those tools. While
  > the results seem similar, they don’t actually use the same language to
  > produce them.

This is a rather disturbing picture.  It suggests that maintaining a
program whose code was generated by LLM is a complex quandry: what
constitutes "the source code"?  Is it the output generated by the LLM,
or is it the input to the LLM system?  Is either of the two really
usable as the source code?

If the output, generated in some programming language, is
understandable as source code, and reasonable to modify,
that is ok.  We could designate that as "the source code".

However, it may be difficult to edit by hand.

The other option is to designate the input to the LLM as the source
code.  But you're saying that the effects of a simple change in that input
may be complex and unpredictable.  So this option, though simple in the
abstract, may be difficult to deal with.

[[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
[[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
[[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]

I am convinced now that we must distinguish between source code that
happened to have come originally from an LLM, and non-source code in
high-level-language, used as an intermediate form generated by an LLM
from source code in some other form.  These are fundamentally
different scenarios and we need to treat them separately.

In the former case, the one-time use of the LLM has no effect _on
further development_, since people working on that code won't have a
reason to care about the LLM.  (The LLM's use _can_ have an effect _on
legal issues_.)  The code needs comments and clarity sufficient for
humans to work on it.

The latter case is like Bison output, where the Bison input is the
source code.  Using such source code is acceptable because Bison is a
released free tool, not limited to use as SaaSS, and acceptable to
require developers to use.  Using LLM input as source code will
require that the specific LLM be free, released, and usable locally,
and acceptable to require developers to use.

This issue is separate from the issues of copyright that LLMs
inherently raise.  We need to heed both issues, but the kinds of
requirements they imply will be different.

On 11/6/26 7:06 AM, Eli Zaretskii wrote:

 > Why is it problematic and inconsiderate?

Such patches would quickly become too complex for everyone involved, and 
the usual back-and-forth that improves a patch cannot happen. The author 
can't reliably reorganize LLM output since they don't understand it, and 
the reviewer can't reconstruct the intent from the prompt, which is 
neither reproducible nor human-readable.

 > Who said forking is the way forward?

Note that the fork is being proposed by those who want an LLM-free 
Emacs, not by those who want LLM code accepted. If accepting LLM code is 
what forces a fork, the ones who want it accepted should be the ones 
forking. The fact that they aren't suggests they expect Emacs to absorb 
the cost for them.

And in another thread someone proposed that LLM-written patches be 
identified, reviewed, classified and accepted, again without proposing a 
fork. So the implicit expectation seems to be that Emacs maintainers 
will sooner or later have to use LLMs themselves, both to write and to 
review code.

If that is what happens, the contribution will not be accepted.  We
will never accept code we don't understand or which is not according
to our conventions.  If the contributor drops the ball because he/she
cannot cope with the burden, then the changes will not be installed
(unless someone else picks up the gauntlet and completes the job).

>  > Who said forking is the way forward?
> 
> Note that the fork is being proposed by those who want an LLM-free

C99?  Or any other decision by the Emacs developers to make some
change in the conventions and procedures?  Are you saying that each
such change requires a fork?  I hope not.

And what costs are you alluding to that need to be considered should
we be allowed to use LLMs in Emacs?  If someone uses LLM to generate
some part of a patch, what costs will that impose on anyone else?

In any case, any such costs, if they exist, will be considered if and
when we are allowed to use LLM-generated code in Emacs.

Let's delay the discussion of what might soon happen until it happens.
We have enough real issues to talk about and work on than hypothetical
changes whose future is at this point uncertain.

On 11/6/26 12:44 PM, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
> And what costs are you alluding to that need to be considered should
> we be allowed to use LLMs in Emacs?  If someone uses LLM to generate
> some part of a patch, what costs will that impose on anyone else?
There are several costs, but I think the most important one here is the 
asymmetry cost.  The author who uses an LLM uses it to reduce the effort 
of understanding the problem, and shifts that effort onto the reviewers 
and accepters of the patch.  Even if the patch is ultimately rejected, 
the reviewer still has to spend the effort to determine that it cannot 
be understood or reorganized, and the author cannot help because they 
don't understand it either.  Moreover, for that effort to be worthwhile 
on the maintainer's side, the maintainer must also be able to produce 
and review code with an LLM, which means they must control that LLM in 
order to be effective as a maintainer.

Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:

> This is a rather disturbing picture.  It suggests that maintaining a
> program whose code was generated by LLM is a complex quandry: what
> constitutes "the source code"?  Is it the output generated by the LLM,
> or is it the input to the LLM system?  Is either of the two really
> usable as the source code?
>
> If the output, generated in some programming language, is
> understandable as source code, and reasonable to modify,
> that is ok.  We could designate that as "the source code".
>
> However, it may be difficult to edit by hand.

I have worked at two different software companies where they have
welcomed in LLM contributions, so I have firsthand experience observing
what happens to a codebase where this is allowed. In both cases, the
developers were very clearly instructed by management to use it
"responsibly" and to keep the source code maintainable.

The developers started out with the best intentions and initially used
it to make edits that were reasonable in scope. But in both cases it
didn't end there; the more they used these systems, the more comfortable
they got with putting them in the driver's seat, and over time the
systems decayed to the point where it was an exhausting feat to try to
understand them.

I would ask my co-workers what a function that they ostensibly wrote was
meant to do, and I'd get blank stares back. Eventually I had to leave
the first company (during the worst job market of my entire life) due to
this problem.

This phenomenon is known as the "vibe bobsled", and it's been well
documented; even people who are enthusiastic LLM users admit it happens:

https://dustycloud.org/blog/faulty-towers-vibe-sickness-and-the-vibe-bobsled/

> At the top of the chute, people tell themselves they're going to use
> these tools as a kind of fancy autocomplete. As they descend, they say
> they'll spin up some agents to explore ideas, but they'll write the
> code themselves. Next their agents are generating the code for them,
> but don't worry, but they'll review all the output. Soon they're
> plummeting downward and well, they don't actually review the code
> being spat out much anymore, but they trust the agents, heck maybe the
> agents are actually better coders than they are they say. And where
> does it go from there? From "I don't even code anymore" to "I don't
> even prompt anymore"?
>
> At every stage of the process, the coder in question removes
> themselves from the process of producing code, and gives in towards a
> faith-based initiative of code production, that the LLM knows and does
> a good job of what it's doing. But what is the source of gravity
> pulling the sled along this icy chute?
>
> It's simple. Generation is not the slow part of
> coding. Theory-building and review are. And plausible-enough things
> are extremely hard to debug and understand. But the machines are so
> fast at producing things. If you are going to review their work, you
> aren't really taking advantage of their most powerful property, which
> is speed. But theory-building and review are also the programmer's
> most important role.

Like with many SaaS products, LLM vendors have been caught admitting
that they deliberately design the flow of these systems with the goal of
being addictive, so it's not particularly surprising that this happens.
The only surprise is that people who should know better continue to fall
for it.

I know this looks at first glance like a slippery slope fallacy, but I'm
just describing what happened from painful firsthand personal experience.
I have read about the same thing happening in multiple free software
projects as well, but I can only speak from firsthand experience what
it's like at work, because the free software projects I contribute to
other than Emacs have already taken steps to ban this.

-Phil

ps. I hesitate to bring this up at all, because I believe the ethical
    issues involved are much, much more serious than the practical
    issues. I believe GNU should have a hardline stance against
    plagiarism, and it's baffling to me that this is controversial! But
    I made an exception here because RMS asked about it specifically.
    Please do not interpret this as implying that it would be OK to
    accept LLM patches if the issues above were somehow comprehensively
    addressed!

> On 11/6/26 12:44 PM, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
> > And what costs are you alluding to that need to be considered should
> > we be allowed to use LLMs in Emacs?  If someone uses LLM to generate
> > some part of a patch, what costs will that impose on anyone else?
> There are several costs, but I think the most important one here is the 
> asymmetry cost.  The author who uses an LLM uses it to reduce the effort 
> of understanding the problem, and shifts that effort onto the reviewers 
> and accepters of the patch.  Even if the patch is ultimately rejected, 
> the reviewer still has to spend the effort to determine that it cannot 
> be understood or reorganized, and the author cannot help because they 
> don't understand it either.

I don't see how this is different from reviewing any other
contribution.  When I review a patch, the amount of effort invested by
the contributor has no effect on my efforts.  And I always need to
invest some effort to understand the changes.

> Moreover, for that effort to be worthwhile on the maintainer's side,
> the maintainer must also be able to produce and review code with an
> LLM, which means they must control that LLM in order to be effective
> as a maintainer.

I don't see why reviewing a patch, any patch, would require to use an
LLM.

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

>> I would ask my co-workers what a function that they ostensibly wrote was
>> meant to do, and I'd get blank stares back. Eventually I had to leave
>> the first company (during the worst job market of my entire life) due to
>> this problem.
>
> When we get a submission of code, we almost always ask questions and
> request some changes.  What do you think will happen if in response we
> get "blank stares"?

The blank stares happen in the workplace because we frequently spend
time in video calls. On a mailing list it's not real-time, so of course
the LLM user would have a chance to copy your questions into their LLM
and feed the slop replies back to you.

It's quite difficult to explain if you haven't experienced it firsthand,
but LLM-generated code and explanations are astonishingly good at
*looking* correct and being extremely convincing at first glance in a
way that is completely disconnected to whether it is correct or not.

Imagine dealing with a never-ending stream of subtly-flawed patches
written by expert liars trying to trick you into accepting them. Your
intuition that you've spent decades building up based on reading code
written by humans is nearly worthless in this case, because it's been
fed trillions of examples of training data of what a convincing reply
looks like and can emit a realistic-looking reproduction of them.

That's the entire strength of an LLM; it can generate convincing-looking
text at an inexhaustible pace. On occasion by luck sometimes it happens
that it aligns with correctness, but it will always *appear* correct.

-Phil

> but LLM-generated code and explanations are astonishingly good at

> written by expert liars trying to trick you into accepting them. Your
> intuition that you've spent decades building up based on reading code
> written by humans is nearly worthless in this case, because it's been
> fed trillions of examples of training data of what a convincing reply
> looks like and can emit a realistic-looking reproduction of them.
> 
> That's the entire strength of an LLM; it can generate convincing-looking
> text at an inexhaustible pace. On occasion by luck sometimes it happens
> that it aligns with correctness, but it will always *appear* correct.

after reading that, if you're still worried we cannot cope with this.

﻿(Replying out of order so that I can cover the biggest things first.)

On 11/3/2026 7:19 AM, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
> Please at least wait until there's some sign of something like that
> happening in Emacs.  It is at least unfair to threaten a fork (which
> 110% sure is a blow to the community -- I'm old enough to remember how
> things were during the XEmacs schism) just because the Linux kernel
> did something we don't like or don't want to happen in our community.

I don't want to fork GNU Emacs either, and absolutely agree that doing 
so would be a blow to the community. However, this is an issue many 
people feel very strongly about, and which affects both how (free) 
software is produced and how community members work together. I fear 
that *any* eventual decision here will cause some parts of the community 
to split off.

For my part, I spoke up in this thread rather than waiting because I 
want to raise these concerns before any serious problems befall the 
Emacs community. Better to calmly evaluate things while we can watch 
other projects' struggles than to be thrown into managing a possible 
future crisis.

> And I'm most alarmed by the suggestion that we should reject someone's
> code based on something that is unrelated to the code itself.  This is
> a step along a slippery slope that I very much hope we will never
> take.  Because the next thing we will be requested is to reject code
> of people with particular views or opinions, or people living under
> certain regimes, etc. etc.  We never did anything like that, and
> IMNSHO we shouldn't, ever.

I don't think our views are so far apart here. It's why in my message, I 
was careful to focus on LLM-assisted contributions instead of LLMs in 
general. In addition to the legal/copyright issues that the FSF is 
already aware of, LLMs significantly alter the way communication 
happens, whether that's code, documentation, or discussions on the 
mailing lists.

Take the recent bug reports from "roelof's assistent", which 
self-reports as an AI. So long as this is a rare occurrence, it's no 
reason to panic, but I imagine it would get frustrating pretty quickly 
if this were a common way to report bugs. At best, it's an extra layer 
between us and the user making it harder to build a human connection; at 
worst, it's spam contributing to maintainer burnout.

Ultimately, while I have my own opnions about LLMs in general, I agree 
that it would be quite a serious change to start rejecting someone's 
contributions for using LLMs in some other context, or even simply 
having different views on them.

> If some contributor decides to use LLMs for developing Emacs code, and
> they do it in a way that prevents them from learning, that is their
> business: the harm, such as it is, will be caused to them and no one
> else.  Our job is to make sure that code that lands in Emacs is
> useful, correct, well-designed and well-implemented.  We cannot be
> held responsible for whatever the contributors do in the privacy of
> their development environment.  I also think it's naïve, to say the
> least, to think that by rejecting LLM-generated code we will affect
> their decision to use LLM.

We wouldn't likely change anyone's mind (certainly not quickly), but we 
*can* do things to encourage participation from the sorts of community 
members we'd like to have.

> We don't require knowledgeable Emacs developers to provide mentoring.
> I personally think we should try (and do try myself), but this is not
> a requirement.

That's true, and I've wanted to provide mentorship for newcomers in a 
more active way, though I'm still thinking about how best to do that. I 
credit the friendliness and mentorship of you, Lars Ingebrigtsen, 
Michael Albinus, and others for why I maintain Eshell now, despite not 
knowing any Lisp as recently as 2021. That's one of the main reasons 
this aspect is so important to me. The mentorship and community in Emacs 
is something everyone here should be proud of.

> So I don't see why the (so far largely theoretical) danger that
> someone will mentor less contributors who use LLMs is so fundamentally
> different from them deciding to mentor less because they have less
> free time or for whatever other reason.

There are a few factors that worry me about the intersection of LLMs and 
mentorship. First, as I mentioned before, is the marketing. If we listen 
to the companies making these products, the intent is for them to 
replace junior developers, and that will be reflected in their design.

Second is their addictive nature: because LLMs are stochastic and don't 
always produce correct results, users experience a variable reward 
schedule, leading to addiction in the same ways gambling can. This often 
leads to overuse at the expense of less immediately-satisfying things, 
like mentoring. (These problems aren't strictly unique to LLMs, but I 
think the risks are elevated with them.)

Third, like you mentioned, the attitude of the mentee counts. A mentee 
who not only wants to learn but also to engage socially is more 
satisfying to mentor. One of the complaints the Linux kernel maintainers 
had was that LLM-using novices are particularly frustrating to mentor, 
which was one of their reasons for deprioritizing mentorship. This is 
partly because they don't learn and partly because they just want their 
name in the kernel changelog.

I don't expect the Emacs maintainers or the community as a whole to make 
a decision on this right away. I also hope you don't see Human Emacs as 
a power play or personality conflict. For me at least, I view it as a 
last resort to preserve a space for people who value the craft of code 
and the community built around it.

Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:

> In the former case, the one-time use of the LLM has no effect _on
> further development_, since people working on that code won't have a
> reason to care about the LLM.

This argment holds if afterwards no one will use LLMs to work on the
code.

An example where this would be the case could be when someone takes up
an abandoned project.
(though this doesn=E2=80=99t resolve the copyright problems)

If non-LLM-use isn=E2=80=99t secured, there is a risk that taking up such a
project creates pressure to use LLMs to work with the code.

Or that it could open the loophole of saying that this project was only
generated as a start and now will be fit for humans =E2=80=93 but then more
LLM-generated changes are added, again creating pressure to use LLMs.

> The code needs comments and clarity sufficient for
> humans to work on it.

This could be stated more in a more general way:
the code should be in suitable shape for humans to work with it.

It should at least be maintainable without pushing people into depending
on SaaSS or proprietary tools to provide the minimum of maintenance
required when pressing matters like security issues come up.

One part is that it should be small enough: with LLMs one human can
within months cause the generation of 100.000 lines of code that do
something. It is unlikely that this amount of LLM-created code could be
understood by a group of humans, and even less likely that it could be
maintained.

This is different with human-written projects, because even if those
grow big, their different parts were at least partially understood by a
human by the time they were written.

> Using LLM input as source code will require that the specific LLM be
> free, released, and usable locally, and acceptable to require
> developers to use.

Another part there is that the input should actually work as source
code. Meaning that the LLM can be run again and no repeat review of the
code is needed. Input in that case would not just be prompts, but the
whole state of the LLM. A minimum question to that would be =E2=80=9Ccan you
reproduce the results from the source code=E2=80=9D. In the past years we (=
as
Free Software community) spent a lot of effort to make most of our
binary builds reproducible. Similar may be needed to use LLMs as a kind
of transpiler.

If the LLM is Free Software, it would also be necessary that its source
is at least provided on request. And the source of current LLMs is
massive: roughly all of the internet, along with filters and "alignment"
measures, plus build tooling to process it in data centers for weeks to
months, likely burning through some expensive GPUs.

Best wishes,
Arne

Unpolitisch sein

ohne es zu merken.

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

> If that is what happens, the contribution will not be accepted.  We
> will never accept code we don't understand or which is not according
> to our conventions.  If the contributor drops the ball because he/she
> cannot cope with the burden, then the changes will not be installed
> (unless someone else picks up the gauntlet and completes the job).

I already experienced how I myself lowered my review standards for an
LLM contribution at work, because the change was obviously useful, and
most of the work had already been invested.

Seeing another person struggle and not wanting to push away a
contributor make it hard not to move the standards. After all we might
also do it for human contributions, just to avoid frustrating a
newcomer who may learn. But that doesn=E2=80=99t work with LLM contribution=
s.

ANd if someone else picks up the gauntlet, the effort shifts from the
original contributor to that someone else.

I do not doubt the intention not to fall for that, but I know how easy
it is to cave in to social pressure =E2=80=93 and be it only the internaliz=
ed
wish not to let someone else struggle in vain.

I=E2=80=99m not saying =E2=80=9Cif I were the reviewer, this wouldn=E2=80=
=99t happen=E2=80=9D, but =E2=80=9CI
already saw myself cave in, do I think that all our reviewers are way
more principled than I am?=E2=80=9D.

Best wishes,
Arne

On 05/11/2026 20:54, Eli Zaretskii wrote:
>> And ultimately, the source code of
>> vibe-spell.el, while unusual, is still editable as such without the user
>> needing access to the C++ source.
> That's also true for C/C++ code generated by Bison, and for Texinfo
> generated from an Org document (as well as in many other similar
> cases), but we still require to include the original source.  I don't
> understand how this case is different.

As a historical analogy, I hear that GCC switched from YACC/Bison 
parsers to hand-written ones, most probably based on the compiled 
outputs of the former.

Regarding the perspective of Hunspell sources diverging, that is a 
concern, but same as any forked version of software would cause. So we 
could apply similar reasoning as when adopting forked software: Is it 
useful and somehow better than the original? Is it likely to continue to 
be maintained (or still acceptable even if not)?.

Den ons 4 nov. 2026 kl 21:23 skrev Augusto Stoffel <arstoffel@gmail.com>:
> Here, for better or worse, the perspective must be a bit different.  I
> didn't ask an LLM to help me write some code; I just made it translate
> from C++ to Elisp, and keep iterating until the Hunspell tests pass and
> the obvious performance bottlenecks are fixed.  The code in a way
> doesn't matter, and I only looked cursorily at it.

But if you only cursory looked at it there is zero quality control.
Honestly, it seems extremely dubious to publish such code in a public
repository such as ELPA, which comes with implied expectations. As a
user of ELPA  I expect that at least some honest humans have looked at
the code. Otherwise what's stopping someone from inserting backdoors
into very long LLM-generated .el files? It's like an editor publishing
letters to the editor without reading them.

> Take the recent bug reports from "roelof's assistent", which

Please re-read one of his bug reports and my responses, and elaborate
why you are alarmed by what you read there.  (But please confine
yourself to what was actually written, not to what could have been
written in some different theoretical case.)

Personally, I found no problems whatsoever to deal with those bug
reports, and I hope you will conclude the same when you read the
exchange carefully.

> > If some contributor decides to use LLMs for developing Emacs code, and
> > they do it in a way that prevents them from learning, that is their
> > business: the harm, such as it is, will be caused to them and no one
> > else.  Our job is to make sure that code that lands in Emacs is
> > useful, correct, well-designed and well-implemented.  We cannot be
> > held responsible for whatever the contributors do in the privacy of
> > their development environment.  I also think it's naïve, to say the
> > least, to think that by rejecting LLM-generated code we will affect
> > their decision to use LLM.
> 
> We wouldn't likely change anyone's mind (certainly not quickly), but we 
> *can* do things to encourage participation from the sorts of community 
> members we'd like to have.

If you mean encouraging people to do things themselves so they learn
better and faster, no one in their right minds will object to that.
Nor would comments to that effect in a discussion of a submission be
out of place, IMO.  But that is a very far cry from what the OP said
when he started this thread, and a very-very-VERY far cry from forking
Emacs.

> > So I don't see why the (so far largely theoretical) danger that
> > someone will mentor less contributors who use LLMs is so fundamentally
> > different from them deciding to mentor less because they have less
> > free time or for whatever other reason.
> 
> There are a few factors that worry me about the intersection of LLMs and 
> mentorship. First, as I mentioned before, is the marketing. If we listen 
> to the companies making these products, the intent is for them to 
> replace junior developers, and that will be reflected in their design.

Well, then don't listen.  (Who would ever listen seriously to any
marketing hype, especially nowadays when a simple Internet search --
which ironically is based on LLMs -- can tell you much more and much
more concisely?)  And tell others to listen less.  What does this have
to do with admitting contributions to Emacs, let alone justify
forking?

> Second is their addictive nature: because LLMs are stochastic and don't 
> always produce correct results, users experience a variable reward 
> schedule, leading to addiction in the same ways gambling can. This often 
> leads to overuse at the expense of less immediately-satisfying things, 
> like mentoring. (These problems aren't strictly unique to LLMs, but I 
> think the risks are elevated with them.)

Once again, if our mentoring falls on deaf ears, it will stop,
regardless of the reasons why the mentee doesn't react well.

> Third, like you mentioned, the attitude of the mentee counts. A mentee 
> who not only wants to learn but also to engage socially is more 
> satisfying to mentor. One of the complaints the Linux kernel maintainers 
> had was that LLM-using novices are particularly frustrating to mentor, 
> which was one of their reasons for deprioritizing mentorship. This is 
> partly because they don't learn and partly because they just want their 
> name in the kernel changelog.

This is again about those people who cannot use LLMs wisely.  It
doesn't affect the Emacs maintainers, who need to deal with such
attitude already, and it doesn't affect Emacs and its code.  I don't
see why we should be responsible for people who are unwise enough to
hurt their own abilities, and I definitely don't see how that could be
stopped by refusing to accept LLM-generated code or by forking Emacs.

> I don't expect the Emacs maintainers or the community as a whole to make 
> a decision on this right away. I also hope you don't see Human Emacs as 
> a power play or personality conflict. For me at least, I view it as a 
> last resort to preserve a space for people who value the craft of code 
> and the community built around it.

I see it as a greatly exaggerated reaction to problems that are
largely if not completely unrelated to Emacs and its development.
Where they could be relevant, they didn't yet happen, and the fears
(at least those I've seen written so far) are based on basic mistrust
of our abilities and intentions as Emacs maintainers.

> From: "Dr. Arne Babenhauserheide" <arne_bab@web.de>
> Cc: eliz@gnu.org,  jporterbugs@gmail.com,  bugs@gnu.support,
>   phil@hagelb.org,  emacs-devel@gnu.org
> Date: Fri, 06 Nov 2026 23:48:36 +0100
> 
> > The code needs comments and clarity sufficient for
> > humans to work on it.
> 
> This could be stated more in a more general way:
> the code should be in suitable shape for humans to work with it.

That goes without saying.  It's a primary goal of reviewing any code
submission.  Stating it explicitly would be silly IMO, because it's
like stating that people should be allowed to breathe.  What we
found useful to say about that we already have in CONTRIBUTE.

> It should at least be maintainable without pushing people into depending
> on SaaSS or proprietary tools to provide the minimum of maintenance
> required when pressing matters like security issues come up.

A large part of our patch review and comments process is to ensure
long-term maintainability of the submitted code.  It's again goes
without saying that this is part of our job as Emacs maintainers,
completely unrelated to the LLM issues.  Because humans can and do
write hard-to-understand code as well.

> One part is that it should be small enough: with LLMs one human can
> within months cause the generation of 100.000 lines of code that do
> something. It is unlikely that this amount of LLM-created code could be
> understood by a group of humans, and even less likely that it could be
> maintained.

No one around here will accept a patch of 100K lines, unless it is
redesigning and reimplementing something at the heart of Emacs, like
the display engine with all of its back-ends.  In which case the new
code is a replacement, and must by itself be well-commented and
understandable by us.  If we cannot understand a submission, we won't
accept it.  So let's not bring up absurd arguments like that.

> This is different with human-written projects, because even if those
> grow big, their different parts were at least partially understood by a
> human by the time they were written.

We the Emacs maintainers need to understand any code that we accept.
Large and significant patches make this more important, not less
important.  So please let's stop these repeated posts that are based
on fears which have no basis whatsoever, and in a way are an insult to
us the Emacs maintainers, because they implicitly assume we don't have
the tools, the experience, and the common sense to deal with such
situations if and when they happen.  Please at least have enough
respect for us to defer publishing such fears until something even
remotely similar actually happens.

> > Using LLM input as source code will require that the specific LLM be
> > free, released, and usable locally, and acceptable to require
> > developers to use.
> 
> Another part there is that the input should actually work as source
> code. Meaning that the LLM can be run again and no repeat review of the
> code is needed. Input in that case would not just be prompts, but the
> whole state of the LLM. A minimum question to that would be “can you
> reproduce the results from the source code”. In the past years we (as
> Free Software community) spent a lot of effort to make most of our
> binary builds reproducible. Similar may be needed to use LLMs as a kind
> of transpiler.

This is something that the GNU Project leadership will need to
consider if and when they lift the ban on including LLM-generated
code.  They will then need to publish the guidance in standards.texi
so that we the maintainers know what to require as prerequisites for
accepting such code.  It is pointless to discuss this here until and
unless GNU does make these decisions, because this is not an Emacs
issue.

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

> Forking is different, at least potentially, because it completely
> severs the relation to the original code, and that original code is
> not needed to make subsequent changes.

Not needed, but often still useful. I would normally expect forkers to
preserve the existing history of the project, so important changes to
the original can easily be cherry-picked into the fork.

As long as the original project isn=E2=80=99t either perfect or dead, I exp=
ect
that such cherry-picking will be required in forks from time to time.

> That is why I asked what would be the workflow for someone to
> "cherry-pick" an upstream change in Hunspell into vibe-spell.  The
> answer should tell us whether the original source is important or not.

It should also tell, what can be seen as source code.

>> >
>> > How would J.R. Hacker (not the original author) who wants to do this

>> > original version are not available?
>>=20
>> I don't think that this is really a hindrance for LLM nowadays, but in
>> any case writing down what version of Hunspell the code was based on
>> will make it easier.
>
> The source code is also the best documentation of the package, and
> AFAIU for that Hunspell is better in this role.

Why should it be?  The source code of Hunspell (or actually Nuspell)
expresses exactly the same algorithms, except that vibe-spell can drop
some of the ceremony around it since it doesn't have to deal with memory
management and being a general library but is specialized and simplified
for Elisp.

>> In either case, this is just a new implementation of a spell checker
>> that happens to have initially been based on a translation from C++.
>
> So is the output of Bison: "a new implementation" of a parser in C or
> C++.

I'd argue that "new implementation" means two different things here.
For Bison, this is a deterministically computed translation where the
output is just an intermediate representation.  If compiling code were
trivial, there is no reason why Bison wouldn't just generate Assembly
directly.  For a translation+fork between languages as different as C++
and Lisp there are design decision that have to be made -- by a human or
an LLM -- that actually make it a "new" implementation.

>> There is no inherent need to backport changes from the original
>> language, if this is not a goal of the project.  If Augusto decides to
>> take the tool in that direction, we shouldn't take that as a reason to
>> reject the package.
>
> It isn't only up to Augusto.  Free Software allows anyone to take a
> project, modify it, and distribute it under a free license.
> Distributing a Free Software package under GPL should allow people
> doing that.

It is up to Augusto whether he views this as a fork that shares a
history but no future with the original project or whether as the
maintainer of the project being back to backport changes from the
upstream project into his codebase is a priority that has to be
accommodated.  If someone forks vibe-code they naturally can pursue a
different policy and ensure that backporting is possible, but that is a
much more difficult task.

>> > Or what if certain paradigms and implementation details of Hunspell
>> > need special considerations or handling when converting them to ELisp,
>> > something that Augusto have learned during his iterative process? do
>> > you expect J.R. Hacker to re-discover them anew?  Does this sound like
>> > "a package with full source code" to you?
>>=20
>> It is interesting that the LLM was instructed to dump parts of the
>> "thought process" inside the file:
>>=20
>> https://github.com/astoff/vibe-spell/blob/04966165445bdacf203ef30d50d167=
6227edac49/vibe-spell.el#L193
>
> That's exactly a part of the stuff which is useful to publish as part
> of the source, so I guess we are now in agreement?

I guess we agree that these notes are useful, what we don't agree on is
whether vibe-code is a fork+translation or not.  I still think that this
is up to the maintainer to decide.

> Den ons 4 nov. 2026 kl 21:23 skrev Augusto Stoffel <arstoffel@gmail.com>:
>> Here, for better or worse, the perspective must be a bit different.  I

>> from C++ to Elisp, and keep iterating until the Hunspell tests pass and
>> the obvious performance bottlenecks are fixed.  The code in a way

>
> But if you only cursory looked at it there is zero quality control.

This couldn't be farther from the truth.

The package passes the Hunspell test suite (with some exceptions that I
understand) and it works with all Hunspell dictionaries distributed in
Debian (with a couple of well-understood exceptions also noted in the
README).

There was also quite a bit of work involved to make the library fast.

> Honestly, it seems extremely dubious to publish such code in a public
> repository such as ELPA, which comes with implied expectations. As a
> user of ELPA  I expect that at least some honest humans have looked at
> the code. Otherwise what's stopping someone from inserting backdoors
> into very long LLM-generated .el files? It's like an editor publishing
> letters to the editor without reading them.

That's a good general point and is a concern I have in other contexts.
But this library doesn't do any IO at all (other than loading
dictionaries).  A "cursory look" is enough to ascertain that fact.

> From: Philip Kaludercic <philipk@posteo.net>
> Cc: yuri.v.khan@gmail.com,  arstoffel@gmail.com,  cwebber@dustycloud.org,
>   emacs-devel@gnu.org

> 
> Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:
> 
> > The source code is also the best documentation of the package, and
> > AFAIU for that Hunspell is better in this role.
> 
> Why should it be?

Because it was written by humans who left behind comments and
meaningful symbol names, and because LLM-driven translation to another
PL doesn't necessarily preserve the comments and names.

> >> In either case, this is just a new implementation of a spell checker
> >> that happens to have initially been based on a translation from C++.
> >
> > So is the output of Bison: "a new implementation" of a parser in C or
> > C++.
> 
> I'd argue that "new implementation" means two different things here.
> For Bison, this is a deterministically computed translation where the
> output is just an intermediate representation.  If compiling code were
> trivial, there is no reason why Bison wouldn't just generate Assembly
> directly.  For a translation+fork between languages as different as C++
> and Lisp there are design decision that have to be made -- by a human or
> an LLM -- that actually make it a "new" implementation.

LLM cannot make design decisions, and I don't see why the determinism
is an important aspect here.

And yes, it is easy to write a script around Bison which will produce
assembly or machine language directly.  The fact that Bison produces C
or C++ is just because of the Unix philosophy of each tool doing a
single job, that's all.  So I don't quite see your point there, nor
why it is relevant in this case.

> >> There is no inherent need to backport changes from the original
> >> language, if this is not a goal of the project.  If Augusto decides to
> >> take the tool in that direction, we shouldn't take that as a reason to
> >> reject the package.
> >
> > It isn't only up to Augusto.  Free Software allows anyone to take a
> > project, modify it, and distribute it under a free license.
> > Distributing a Free Software package under GPL should allow people
> > doing that.
> 
> It is up to Augusto whether he views this as a fork that shares a
> history but no future with the original project or whether as the
> maintainer of the project being back to backport changes from the
> upstream project into his codebase is a priority that has to be
> accommodated.  If someone forks vibe-code they naturally can pursue a
> different policy and ensure that backporting is possible, but that is a
> much more difficult task.

My focus was not on what Augusto intends to do, but what we as Emacs
maintainers are obliged to do when we distribute packages.  AFAIU,
distribution of a package under GPL requires us to make sure the full
sources are available for anyone who'd want to develop the package
for whatever reasons.  "Full sources" in this context means everything
needed to regenerate the final program from its original source form,
with or without modifications.

Anyway, I will now bow out of this discussion and leave the ground for
RMS to clarify our obligations in such cases.  What I wrote was based
on my understanding of what the GPL requires, and it's quite clear
that you and Augusto have a different interpretation.

(I'd b interested in hearing Stefan's and Sean's opinions as well, if
they want to voice them.)

Richard Stallman <rms@gnu.org> writes:

> [[[ To any NSA and FBI agents reading my email: please consider    ]]]
> [[[ whether defending the US Constitution against all enemies,     ]]]
> [[[ foreign or domestic, requires you to follow Snowden's example. ]]]
>
> proof-general has the summary "A generic Emacs interface for proof
> assistants", but no description.    Can someone please explain
> what job this does, and what a "proof assistant" does?

Proof assistants is a different word for theorem provers, and Proof
General is just an Emacs interface for using proof assistants such as
Rocq (formerly known as Coq).

You don't have to restrict yourself to just the short description of a
package btw, you can also read the longer description that mentions this
using the `describe-package' command.

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

>> From: Philip Kaludercic <philipk@posteo.net>
>> Cc: yuri.v.khan@gmail.com,  arstoffel@gmail.com,  cwebber@dustycloud.org,
>>   emacs-devel@gnu.org
>> Date: Sat, 07 Nov 2026 09:52:37 +0000
>> 
>> Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:
>> 
>> > The source code is also the best documentation of the package, and
>> > AFAIU for that Hunspell is better in this role.
>> 
>> Why should it be?
>
> Because it was written by humans who left behind comments and
> meaningful symbol names, and because LLM-driven translation to another
> PL doesn't necessarily preserve the comments and names.

In general yes, it is possible but whether or not this is the case for
vibe-spell has to be decided based on the concrete evidence of the
translation.

>> >> In either case, this is just a new implementation of a spell checker
>> >> that happens to have initially been based on a translation from C++.
>> >
>> > So is the output of Bison: "a new implementation" of a parser in C or
>> > C++.
>> 
>> I'd argue that "new implementation" means two different things here.
>> For Bison, this is a deterministically computed translation where the
>> output is just an intermediate representation.  If compiling code were
>> trivial, there is no reason why Bison wouldn't just generate Assembly
>> directly.  For a translation+fork between languages as different as C++
>> and Lisp there are design decision that have to be made -- by a human or
>> an LLM -- that actually make it a "new" implementation.
>
> LLM cannot make design decisions, and I don't see why the determinism
> is an important aspect here.

Of course they can, or at least do something that to all appearances is
functionally equivalent to design decisions.

You are right that "determinism" is the wrong word here, this is more
about knowing how the procedure of translating works (as an algorithm)
or whether is it something opaque, like the mind of a human being or an
LLM.

> And yes, it is easy to write a script around Bison which will produce
> assembly or machine language directly.  The fact that Bison produces C
> or C++ is just because of the Unix philosophy of each tool doing a
> single job, that's all.  So I don't quite see your point there, nor
> why it is relevant in this case.

The point is that the output of Bison is just an intermediate
representation in a well-understood compilation pipeline.  You can
decide whether or not to keep the generated C file around or not, but
beyond debugging, that is mostly just an interest of caching.  A
translation of the kind we are discussing is _not_ an intermediate
representation.

>> >> There is no inherent need to backport changes from the original
>> >> language, if this is not a goal of the project.  If Augusto decides to
>> >> take the tool in that direction, we shouldn't take that as a reason to
>> >> reject the package.
>> >
>> > It isn't only up to Augusto.  Free Software allows anyone to take a
>> > project, modify it, and distribute it under a free license.
>> > Distributing a Free Software package under GPL should allow people
>> > doing that.
>> 
>> It is up to Augusto whether he views this as a fork that shares a
>> history but no future with the original project or whether as the
>> maintainer of the project being back to backport changes from the
>> upstream project into his codebase is a priority that has to be
>> accommodated.  If someone forks vibe-code they naturally can pursue a
>> different policy and ensure that backporting is possible, but that is a
>> much more difficult task.
>
> My focus was not on what Augusto intends to do, but what we as Emacs
> maintainers are obliged to do when we distribute packages.  AFAIU,
> distribution of a package under GPL requires us to make sure the full
> sources are available for anyone who'd want to develop the package
> for whatever reasons.  "Full sources" in this context means everything
> needed to regenerate the final program from its original source form,
> with or without modifications.

I understand that, the argument I am trying to make is that
vibe-spell.el on its own constitutes the "full sources" you need to make
any changes to the program.  It is in no form reliant on the original
source code that were used to perform the translation.  If you or the
others agree that we wouldn't impose this kind of a requirement on a
human-translated program, then I do not see why this would be the case
for a LLM translated program either.

> Anyway, I will now bow out of this discussion and leave the ground for
> RMS to clarify our obligations in such cases.  What I wrote was based
> on my understanding of what the GPL requires, and it's quite clear
> that you and Augusto have a different interpretation.
>
> (I'd b interested in hearing Stefan's and Sean's opinions as well, if
> they want to voice them.)

1+

Eli Zaretskii <eliz@gnu.org> writes:

> uphold, the ethics of their day-to-day activities, their views on
> matters of policies and important international events, etc.  This
> will immediately fracture our community into many different enclaves.

I consider this a very real risk, and if Human Emacs were to go into
that direction, I wouldn=E2=80=99t think it a good initiative.

And social dynamics may drive it into that direction. In that case I=E2=80=
=99d
have to leave it. Not because I want causes I find apalling to be
supported, but because I think that GNU would not have survived if it
had taken sides on anything but software freedom.

> And that's exactly my point, and the main reason why I must reject the
> "Human Emacs" initiative, as it is presented to us.

I hope that the points I presented do not fit into that: I see actual
problems within code and programming crop up, independent of political
positions.

But I already gave these points and don=E2=80=99t want to walk in circles, =
so I
agree that the next step is to see how GNU policy will be shaped.

I=E2=80=99m glad that we managed to discuss mostly constructively and frien=

Phil Hagelberg <phil@hagelb.org> writes:

> This phenomenon is known as the "vibe bobsled", and it's been well
> documented; even people who are enthusiastic LLM users admit it happens:
>
> https://dustycloud.org/blog/faulty-towers-vibe-sickness-and-the-vibe-bobsled/

> [...]

> I know this looks at first glance like a slippery slope fallacy, but I'm
> just describing what happened from painful firsthand personal experience.

(I'm the author of the quoted blogpost)

On that note, the observation discussed in the blogpost of a growing
amount of code that nobody understands leading to eventually
surrendering to the LLM to explain things came from an LLM *proponent*,
which I used as the frame. Whereas I described a bobsled, the original
proponent described a growing tower... Armin Ronacher, one of the
biggest generative AI via LLM in coding proponents currently around
wrote a blogpost called "The Tower Keeps Rising":

  https://lucumr.pocoo.org/2026/7/13/the-tower-keeps-rising/

In it, Armin describes that AI-assisted codebases eventually become
incomprehensible to human participants, and that they keep growing,
and this is not unlike the tower of babel, which as it grows the
people involved cannot communicate with each other. However, Armin said
this is no problem, for the LLM which is generating the code itself
provides the solution: instead of you, the human, deigning to understand
the codebase, you eventually come to rely on the AI to explain something
when you need it explained. And so it is no problem that we stop
communicating with each other, that humans become less involved with the
process: the tower keeps rising, and when you need to understand
something, you ask the LLM-AI based agent instead.

This was from a *proponent*, mind you.

So the main difference between my blogpost describing the "vibe bobsled"
and Armin's is that Armin is a proponent, and described this as upward
growth. But myself, being worried about communities and the individual
of people to communicate, describe it as downward movement.

In both cases, Armin and I do agree on something: that codebases which
use these things become incomprehensible to people, who come to rely on
AI agents to instead take over. It's merely whether you consider that
upward progress or downward decline that we disagree on.

 - Christine
